name: Peptide stacks (Wolverine stack)

lead: The Wolverine stack pairs BPC-157, a gastric-derived peptide, with TB-500, a thymosin beta-4 fragment. Users take it to speed recovery from injuries and hard training so they can keep lifting, and looksmaxxing forums sometimes extend peptide stacks to skin, bone or height.

The chain is recovery: faster tissue repair means less downtime, more consistent training and more muscle over time. In animal studies BPC-157 shows tissue-protective effects and promotes blood-vessel growth, and thymosin beta-4 binds actin and promotes cell migration. Human evidence is limited to a few small studies, and none addresses appearance.

paras: Users describe running the pair as a recovery protocol around injuries or heavy training blocks, alongside rehab and normal lifting. Products are sold as research peptides.
No regulator has approved BPC-157; health authorities cite insufficient safety data and a theoretical tumour concern. It is banned by WADA, and grey-market products are unregulated.

angle.text: Users pair BPC-157 with TB-500 to speed tissue repair, cut downtime and keep training consistently for more muscle. Support comes from animal studies and a few small human studies, none on appearance.

lead: A peptide stack is a combination of several peptides used together. The best-known recovery pairing is the "Wolverine stack", a nickname for BPC-157 plus TB-500, which proponents link to faster repair of tendons, joints and muscle and to quicker recovery between training sessions.[1][2] The name evokes the fast-healing comic-book character. In looksmaxxing communities, "peptide stack" is also a broader label that can include growth-hormone secretagogues such as CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, the copper peptide GHK-Cu, and weight-loss peptides, discussed for body composition, skin quality, bone mass or height.[3][4][5]

The appearance chain people describe is mostly indirect: recovery peptides are meant to help injuries and sore joints heal so that training can continue, which supports muscle gain and a leaner physique, while GHK-Cu is discussed for skin, and secretagogues for body composition. Teenagers on forums sometimes ask whether stacks might add height or facial bone mass while growth plates or sutures remain open.[3][4]

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide whose discovery was published in 1993 by Predrag Sikirić's group in Zagreb; Wikipedia states that it is not approved by any drug regulator for human use and that human data are scarce.[1] TB-500 is described in anti-doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region of thymosin beta-4, a 44-amino-acid protein studied in cell and animal work and in phase 2 trials of topical and eye products.[2] Two systematic reviews of the human literature on BPC-157 were published in 2025 and 2026.[6][7] No clinical study has tested the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination, or either peptide, for facial appearance, bone mass or height.

paras: BPC-157, also called body protection compound 157, is derived from a protein found in human gastric juice.[1] Preclinical studies, mostly in rodents, describe cytoprotective, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects and possible acceleration of tissue healing; it promotes blood-vessel formation in animals.[1] Reported elimination half-life in rats after injection was between roughly 8 and 30 minutes, and the peptide has been described as stable in human gastric juice for more than a day.[1] Detection methods for urine tests were published in 2017.[1]

Thymosin beta-4 is a 44-residue protein encoded by the TMSB4X gene. It forms a 1:1 complex with G-actin, buffering actin monomers, and in laboratory studies it promotes cell migration, blood-vessel formation and stem-cell maturation while lowering pro-inflammatory cytokines.[2] TB-500 itself receives little coverage in encyclopedic sources and appears mainly in doping literature as a synthetic version of an active region of the protein.[2]

Other peptides that appear in forum stacks are growth-hormone secretagogues, drugs that stimulate growth-hormone release through the ghrelin (GHSR) or growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor. Ipamorelin is listed as a GHSR agonist and CJC-1295 (with or without a DAC modification) as a GHRH receptor agonist; their established clinical role for this drug class is the treatment of growth hormone deficiency, and the class also raises IGF-1, prolactin and cortisol.[5]

The complete sequence of thymosin beta-4 was determined and synthesised in 1981, and the gene was characterised in 1989.[2] Sikirić's group, now emeritus at the University of Zagreb School of Medicine, published BPC-157 in 1993; later milestones in the literature include a rat Achilles tendon study in 2003, a ligament study in 2010, and a preclinical safety evaluation in 2020.[1]

subs.h: Doping cases that publicised thymosin beta-4
paras: In Australia, sports scientist Stephen Dank ran an injection-based supplement program at Essendon from November 2011 that included a substance listed as "thymosin".[8] The Australian Football League tribunal found 34 players not guilty in March 2015, but in January 2016 the Court of Arbitration for Sport, on a World Anti-Doping Agency appeal, found them guilty of using thymosin beta-4 and imposed two-year bans; the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed the players' appeal in October 2016.[8] A separate Cronulla Sharks inquiry in rugby league concerned other peptides, CJC-1295 and GHRP-6, which Dank admitted were injected into players.[9]

Wikipedia says BPC-157 gained popularity among athletes and the general public for injury recovery and that it is used in functional medicine.[1] On looksmax.org, threads from 2025 show users requesting feedback on peptide stacks and posting Wolverine-stack threads, alongside stacks built from secretagogues and GHK-Cu.[3][4][10] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing reports that GHK-Cu has gained virality, that some people inject it from unregulated sources, and that the FDA has warned about the lack of human testing of the injectable form.[11]

Forum threads present stacks as menus: a recovery pair, a secretagogue pair, a copper peptide for skin and sometimes a fat-loss peptide, with posters asking others to critique the combination.[3][4] Typical stated goals include body-fat reduction, clearer or firmer skin, and, among younger posters, height or facial bone mass.[3][4] Replies range from enthusiastic to sceptical; in one thread a respondent says secretagogues release much less growth hormone than the hormone itself and that GHK-Cu mainly helps skin that is already fairly clear.[3]
These are individual reports and opinions. This wiki does not reproduce amounts, schedules or sourcing.

Per Wikipedia, human safety data for BPC-157 are insufficient, health authorities discourage its use, and because it promotes angiogenesis some reviewers raise a theoretical concern that it could promote or enlarge undetected cancers.[1] The 2025 systematic review in HSS Journal reported that no clinical safety data were found and warned of adverse effects from unregulated manufacturing.[6]

WADA added BPC-157 to the prohibited list in 2022 under category S0, and thymosin beta-4 is banned as a recovery aid that may permit heavier training.[1][2] Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (April 2024) and New Zealand's Medsafe (June 2025) moved to control BPC-157 as a prescription medicine, although it is not in practice available by prescription.[1]

In the United States, Wikipedia reports an HHS enforcement-discretion policy dated 10 October 2026 and a 30 October 2026 announcement by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that BPC-157 and five other peptides (TB-500, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c and semax) could be supplied by compounding pharmacies; the peptide remains unapproved by the FDA.[1] The same article lists the approval gap, the cancer concern, the prescription-status contradiction and the fact that much key work comes from the discoverer's own group among the controversies.[1]

No studies found of the BPC-157 plus TB-500 combination. For BPC-157 alone, a 2025 systematic review covering literature to June 2024 included 36 studies, 35 preclinical and one clinical: a retrospective report in which 7 of 12 patients with chronic knee pain reported relief lasting over six months.[6] A 2026 PRISMA-registered review searching to June 2026 found three human studies with 30 participants in total (intra-articular injections for knee pain, an intravesical pilot in interstitial cystitis, and an intravenous safety pilot); most participants reported symptom improvement and no treatment-related adverse events, the studies were of poor methodological quality, certainty was rated very low, and the authors concluded BPC-157 should not be used clinically outside approved high-quality trials.[7] Wikipedia also lists a small 2021 intra-articular study and a phase I trial whose results were not submitted.[1]

Thymosin beta-4 has been studied in phase 2 trials for pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa, reported to speed repair and be well tolerated, and in dry-eye and neurotrophic keratopathy; heart-repair trials are described as ongoing.[2] None of these studies measured facial appearance, bone mass or height.

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org discuss peptide stacks as options for recovery, skin, body composition and, among younger posters, height or bone mass; the Wolverine stack is the recovery pairing most often named.[3][4][10]

timeline.event: Complete sequence of thymosin beta-4 determined and synthesised.[2]
Sikirić's group publishes BPC-157 in the Journal of Physiology, Paris.[1]
Rat Achilles tendon study reports accelerated healing with BPC-157.[1]
Stephen Dank's injection program begins at Essendon, including a substance listed as thymosin.[8]
Court of Arbitration for Sport finds 34 Essendon players guilty of thymosin beta-4 use; Swiss Federal Supreme Court upholds the bans in October.[8]
WADA adds BPC-157 to the prohibited list under S0.[1]
Australia's TGA moves to control BPC-157 as a prescription medicine; a first systematic review of orthopaedic use of BPC-157 follows in 2025.[1][6]
New Zealand's Medsafe reviews and controls BPC-157; looksmax.org peptide-stack threads appear.[1][3][4][10]
A second systematic review of human BPC-157 evidence is published (October); on 30 October HHS announces compounding pharmacies may supply BPC-157 and five other peptides.[1][7]
